related_questions.question: What does CPR do to your body?
related_questions.snippet: CPR can keep oxygen-rich blood flowing to the brain and other organs until emergency medical treatment can get the heart beating again. When the heart stops, the body no longer gets oxygen-rich blood. The lack of oxygen-rich blood can cause brain damage in only a few minutes.

text_blocks.snippet: CPR can be life-saving, but it does have potential side effects and complications. These include physical injuries like broken ribs and sternum, and neurological problems, especially if there is a delay in restoring oxygen to the brain. Other complications can include vomiting, aspiration, internal bleeding, and lung injuries.
snippet_highlighted_words: physical injuries like broken ribs and sternum, and neurological problems

list.snippet: Rib and Sternum Fractures: Chest compressions during CPR can cause fractures of the ribs and sternum.
Muscle and Joint Pain: Chest compressions can lead to muscle soreness and joint pain.
Internal Bleeding: In rare cases, CPR can cause internal bleeding due to damaged blood vessels or organs.
Other Injuries: Rarely, CPR may cause injuries to the lungs, liver, or spleen.

list.title: Brain Damage:
list.snippet: Lack of oxygen to the brain during cardiac arrest can lead to brain damage if CPR is not initiated quickly.

list.title: Neurological Symptoms:
list.snippet: Some survivors may experience neurological symptoms such as tingling, weakness, or cognitive problems.
Vomiting and Aspiration: CPR can cause stomach contents to be vomited and potentially inhaled into the lungs.
Lung Injuries: Pneumothorax (collapsed lung) or lung contusions can occur.
Fatigue: CPR can be physically exhausting for both the person receiving it and the rescuer.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that the potential benefits of CPR in saving a life far outweigh the risks of these complications.
